title: Many words for love
hook: Greek philia and agape, Hebrew chesed, Arabic mahabba, Sanskrit bhakti: each with its own flavor

segments.voice: Yesterday, death close: sixty days ended. Your line was live, then. Did you do one ordinary thing awake? This week thanked a body, watched a sunset end, woke up thankful, welcomed a birth, kept the answers apart and stepped outside. Today, a new question: love. Day eight hundred nineteen.

English makes one word work very hard. The same love goes to a spouse, a grandmother, a best friend, a dog, a city, a song and a sandwich. Nobody is confused, exactly, but a lot gets packed into four letters. Other languages, and the traditions that speak them, keep several words on the shelf, each with its own flavor. So the love block opens there: not with a definition, but with a handful of words, each from its own home, each naming something the others don't.
screen: `ONE WORD, WORKING HARD.` → `SEVERAL WORDS ON THE SHELF.`

segments.voice: First, two Greek words. Philia is the love of friends, the warmth of people who choose each other. Aristotle writes about it at length, and we'll meet him in a few days. Agape is a word the New Testament uses for the love of God and of neighbor. The first letter of John says, "God is love," and the Greek word there is agape. Second, a Hebrew word. Chesed is loyal, steady kindness, love that keeps its promises. The King James Bible renders it more than one way, often as mercy or lovingkindness. Psalm 136 repeats it again and again: "for his mercy endureth for ever." Third, an Arabic word. Mahabba is love, and Sufi writers in Islam used it for the love between God and the seeker. The Qur'an speaks of a people whom God loves and who love Him. Fourth, a Sanskrit word. Bhakti is devotion, love turned toward God. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says that whoever offers him even a leaf, a flower, a fruit or a little water with devotion, he accepts it. Each word has a home, and a flavor you lose if you swap it for another. They aren't five labels for one thing. They're different loves, named by people who noticed something particular about each.
screen: `TWO GREEK WORDS.` · `CHESED, LOYAL KINDNESS.` · `MAHABBA, IN SUFI WRITING.` · `BHAKTI, DEVOTION.` · then, large: `MANY WORDS FOR LOVE.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let your breath settle. Now bring to mind the loves in your life, one at a time, and see which word fits each. A friend you chose: maybe philia. Someone you've stayed loyal to through hard years: maybe chesed. A love that reaches toward something larger, if you have one: maybe bhakti or mahabba. A plain wish for a stranger's good: maybe agape. There's no right answer, and no need to find every kind. Just notice how many loves are already there. The bell holds the time.
Many words for love. Philia, agape, chesed, mahabba, bhakti: each a love with its own home and its own flavor. Today's word.
Your line: many words. Today, each time you say love, pause half a second and ask which kind you mean. Day eight hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: Each tradition has its own vocabulary of love: Christians speak of agape, Jews of chesed, Sufi Muslims of mahabba, Hindus of bhakti, and the Greek philosophers of philia. Each is taught and practiced in its own setting.

fork.reveal: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, a little water. in bhakti, the devotion is what counts, not the size of the gift.

original.note: Hebrew: loyal, steady kindness; the King James Bible often renders it mercy or lovingkindness.

trapdoor: what you thought: love is love; the word doesn't matter.
what it means: traditions named different loves: friendship, loyal kindness, devotion, the love of God and neighbor.
what a scholar hears: one English word stands in for several, so when a translation says love, it's worth asking which word sits underneath.
